All That's Interesting: How Serial Killer Eric Edgar Cooke Terrorized 1960s Australia

content.p: For about five years around the turn of the 1960s a man nobody suspected shot, stabbed, strangled and ran down strangers in the suburbs of Perth, Western Australia. Police later learned that he was a truck driver and father of seven named Eric Edgar Cooke. The city called him the Night Caller. He was convicted of wilful murder in November 1963 and hanged at Fremantle Prison on 26 October 1964, the last execution carried out in the State.

The case did not end with the gallows. Before his arrest two young men, John Button and Darryl Beamish, had already been convicted of killings that Cooke afterwards confessed to. Courts refused for decades to believe him. Button's conviction was quashed in 2002 and Beamish's in 2005, leaving Cooke's story tied to one of the longest-running miscarriages of justice in Australian history.

Cooke was born on 25 February 1931 in Victoria Park, the eldest of three children. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says he went to five schools and, from 14, took a series of semi-skilled jobs. It describes a boy tormented at school over a cleft palate and a hare lip, brutalised by a father he never loved, often hospitalised with head injuries and headaches, and at one point admitted to an asylum. The popular account on All That's Interesting adds that he walked the streets at night to avoid his father's beatings.

He had convictions for theft, breaking and entering and arson before he was an adult. He enlisted in the regular army in the spring of 1952, only to be discharged that August once his record came to light. On 14 October 1953 he married Sally Lavin, a 19-year-old waitress. They had seven children; the dictionary notes that the eldest was intellectually disabled and another was born with a deformed arm.

According to a 2013 retrospective in The West Australian, which interviewed survivors, Cooke's first act of violence came on 12 September 1958. He ran down a 26-year-old Dutch immigrant, Nel Schneider, with a stolen car as she cycled through Bentley. The injury left her with severe epilepsy. In his later confession he wrote that he did it "in the desire to hurt her or anyone".

The pattern that followed had no obvious signature. The dictionary and the newspaper between them describe hit-and-run attacks with stolen cars, home invasions, stabbings and strangling. In one case a 19-year-old, Glenys Peak, was struck on a street in Bayswater in April 1960. She later said she had known her attacker, who had given her lifts to the station and talked mostly about his disabled son. The state later held Cooke responsible for the stabbing of a South Perth beautician on 30 January 1959 and the strangling of a social worker in West Perth on 16 February 1963, both listed in the dictionary.
All That's Interesting reports that he stole a car almost every night, since keys were often left in ignitions in those years, and usually returned it before dawn.

The city's fear sharpened in the early hours of 27 January 1963, after the Australia Day holiday. A series of random shootings with a .22 rifle left Perth's western suburbs in shock. The West Australian says Cooke shot at a couple parked near the Cottesloe Civic Centre, wounding both. Nicholas August was hit in the back of the neck, and the bullet lodged in Rowena Reeves's wrist after she pushed his head down. Cooke then climbed on to a garage roof in Broome Street and shot 29-year-old accountant Brian Weir through open doors. His last two victims that night, it says, were an 18-year-old student, John Sturkey, and a retired grocer, George Walmsley, 55. Both died from gunshot wounds to the head.

The sources differ over Weir. The dictionary describes the accountant as fatally wounded. The West Australian says he lay in a coma for six months, woke, and lived on blind in one eye, deaf in one ear, paralysed down the right side and unable to speak, according to his brother Colin.

The dictionary also records two further murders a fortnight later, which brought a different man, Brian William Robinson, to the gallows after he faced trial on one of the two charges. Public anxiety was already high. The dictionary says the unsolved crimes changed the city's habits: gunsmiths and locksmiths did brisk business, police and politicians were widely criticised, and the casual habits of an easygoing town were over.

All That's Interesting states that police fingerprinted more than 30,000 males over the age of 12 and test-fired more than 60,000 .22 rifles. It gives no source for these figures, so treat them as a popular claim.

The shootings stopped and then returned. In August 1963 an 18-year-old female student was shot in the head while babysitting at Dalkeith. A rifle found hidden in a bush became the key, and the dictionary says Cooke was captured on 1 September when he came back to retrieve the hidden weapon. All That's Interesting adds that police had replaced it with a lookalike tied down with fishing line and then waited. It says he came 17 days after the bush was staked out, though the dictionary gives no such detail.

Cooke first denied the crimes, that article says, but soon confessed. By the account of Estelle Blackburn, the journalist who later investigated his case, he admitted 22 violent crimes: eight murders and 14 attempted murders and assaults, committed between September 1958 and September 1963. The West Australian counts eight murders and 14 other victims, and says Carmel Read, 20, survived when he stabbed her with her own umbrella inside her Nedlands flat and she kicked and screamed until he ran.

He was tried from 25 November 1963 for a single murder, that of Sturkey. His counsel argued he was not guilty by reason of insanity. The dictionary says the defence claimed schizophrenia, which was rejected by Dr A. S. Ellis, the director of mental health services. It also says the state allowed no other psychiatric specialist to examine him. The jury convicted him and the death sentence was pronounced on 27 November.

It adds that there was little public protest against the sentence, though opponents of capital punishment had organised against others in previous cases. Only one woman kept a vigil outside the prison on the morning of his execution.

Blackburn writes that the hanging took place at 8 a.m. on a Monday, 26 October 1964, and was the final use of the death penalty in Western Australia. Fremantle Prison's own history says the gallows built in 1888 were the only place of legal execution in the State until 1984, when the State Parliament passed legislation abolishing the death penalty. Cooke was buried in an unmarked grave at Fremantle cemetery.

The prison's collection holds a rope that a former senior prison officer alleges was used in the hanging. Collections WA records the claim as an allegation, not an established fact. Its entry and the prison's history also differ on the count of those hanged at the gallows: the history says 43 men and one woman, the collection entry 42 men and one woman.
content.h2: Two men in prison for his crimes
content.p: Among the crimes Cooke confessed to were two for which others had already been convicted. Blackburn says detectives declared him a liar when he described, in detail, the February 1963 hit-and-run death of 17-year-old Rosemary Anderson and the December 1959 axe killing of Jillian Brewer, a 22-year-old Melbourne heiress.

John Button, Anderson's 19-year-old boyfriend, had been convicted of manslaughter in May 1963 and sentenced to ten years' hard labour; the jury had set aside a wilful murder charge. Darryl Beamish, also 19, deaf and unable to speak, had been convicted of Brewer's murder in 1961 and sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment. According to Blackburn, both men had signed confessions after long police interviews without parents or lawyers, and both said they had been bullied into them. The 2005 judgment records that Beamish had been in custody on unrelated charges when he was taken to Brewer's flat and questioned.

Cooke repeated his confessions to a lawyer acting for Beamish, in an affidavit in December 1963 and, the court was told, to the prison chaplain, the Reverend Jenkins, whose statement said Cooke made admissions up to the day of his execution, including 15 minutes before it. Their appeals failed. In 1964 the State's Court of Criminal Appeal, and then the High Court, declined to send either case back to a jury to weigh Cooke's confessions. The Chief Justice, Sir Albert Wolff, called him "a villainous unscrupulous liar", according to the dictionary, and said, according to the 2005 judgment, that the nature of his crimes "stamps him as a monster". The judge also suggested that Cooke's retractions, in both cases, may have been an attempt to delay his own execution. Beamish lost a further appeal to the Privy Council in 1965.

The turning point was Blackburn's book Broken Lives, published in November 1998 after what she calls six and a half years of research. Her memoir says it contained enough fresh evidence to move the government to grant new appeals to both men. In Button's case, she says, key evidence came from a police vehicle examiner who had inspected Button's car in 1963 and from a crash reconstruction expert, Rusty Haight, who ran pedestrian impact tests in Perth in February 2000.

On 25 February 2002 the Court of Criminal Appeal quashed Button's conviction; Chief Justice David Malcolm described a miscarriage of justice, Blackburn writes. She adds that it was the longest-standing conviction overturned in Australia, and the first time an Australian court accepted propensity evidence. Western Australia paid Button $460,000 in 2003.

In June 2002 the Attorney General, Jim McGinty, referred Beamish's petition to the court, saying much of his evidence had been accepted in Button's case as raising serious doubts about his conviction. Beamish's sixth appeal was heard in October 2004. On 1 April 2005 the court quashed the conviction.

The 2005 judgment sets out why. It held that the evidence of Cooke's other early-morning home invasions on young women would have been admissible at Beamish's trial. It recorded Beamish's contentions that police documents corroborated his claim of being prompted during questioning and that a detective's trial evidence had been "palpably untrue" on one point. It also called it unfortunate that the prosecutor told the jury, without evidence, that police had been unable to find any means of entry until Beamish showed one, when a memo showed that an officer had already worked out how a key could be pushed out and reached from outside. The court noted, too, that Cooke's confession to the chaplain came shortly before his death.

Later, under a government of a different party, the State gave Beamish an ex gratia payment of $425,000. Attorney General Christian Porter said there was no conclusive finding of significant misconduct by prosecutors or police, that the case against Beamish had been "very strong" in 1964, but that his conviction had been upheld when it was legally unsafe to do so.

The dictionary notes that the atmosphere of the time, with a city hunted by an unknown killer, is reflected in Tim Winton's 1991 novel Cloudstreet. The Law Society of Western Australia has staged an exhibition on the cases of Button and Beamish, including Jenkins's statement of Cooke's last words. Cooke's own record remains unusually well documented because he confessed repeatedly, and the courts that finally believed him did so four decades after he first spoke.
